subject: chemistry
title: Reactants to Products
welcome_lead: Watch matter rearrange itself: old substances vanish and new ones appear.
meta_desc: Understand reactants and products in chemical reactions in this KS3 chemistry adventure.
final_note: You can now read a chemical equation like a story.

concepts.def: Reactants are used up; products are formed in a reaction.
No atoms are lost or made, so total mass stays the same.
Represent reactions; symbol equations must be balanced.
Reactions that release or absorb energy.
Speeds up a reaction without being used up.

walkthroughs.body_html:
A chemical reaction takes one or more substances and turns them into new substances with new properties.

Reactants → Products

Reactants go on the left, products go on the right, and an arrow shows the direction of change.

Example: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.

When you burn magnesium, you see a bright white flame and a white powder forms.

magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide

The shiny metal has gone; a totally new white solid is made.

mcqs.q: What do we call the new substances made in a reaction?
options: Reactants
Products
Mixtures
Elements

mcqs.q: In the equation 'iron + sulfur → iron sulfide', what is iron?
options: A product
A reactant
A mixture
A solution

mcqs.q: How do alkenes typically react with bromine?
options: The alkene polymerises with bromine to form a long chain.
Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.
Bromine substitutes for a hydrogen on the alkene, releasing HBr.
By electrophilic addition — bromine adds across the double bond to form a dibromoalkane.

mcqs.q: Can a single standard electrode potential be measured in isolation?
options: No — electrode potentials are RELATIVE values measured against a reference (the standard hydrogen electrode, defined as 0 V).
Each electrode has an absolute potential that can be measured directly with a voltmeter.
Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.
The alkene polymerises with bromine to form a long chain.

mcqs.q: What happens to electrons when sodium reacts with chlorine?
options: Protons move from chlorine to sodium to balance the charges.
Sodium and chlorine share an electron between them.
Sodium loses one electron to chlorine; the resulting Na+ and Cl- ions attract electrostatically.
Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.
